title: How IB Grade Boundaries Are Set
summary: How IB grade boundaries are set, why thresholds change between sessions, and how marks become grades. A clear guide for IB students and parents.
body_markdown:
A student sees 68% at the top of a marked assessment and feels a familiar jolt. Is that a 6? A 7? Has the exam gone well, or merely looked respectable?


The honest answer is that the percentage alone cannot tell them.


**How IB grade boundaries are set** comes down to a review of the quality of students’ work against established grade descriptors. Experienced examiners use professional judgement, supported by statistical evidence and feedback about the assessment, to decide the mark thresholds separating grades 1-7. The boundaries are set for a particular subject, level, component and examination session. They are not one permanent percentage scale applied across the entire Diploma Programme.


That is the short answer. Understanding the process beneath it makes an IB result feel less mysterious and helps students use boundaries intelligently rather than trying to predict them.


### IB grade boundaries at a glance


- A **mark** records performance on an assessment.
- A **grade boundary** is the threshold at which one grade becomes another.
- Candidate work is considered against published grade descriptors.
- Examiner judgement is supported by statistical and assessment evidence.
- Boundaries may change when the difficulty or demands of an assessment change.
- Different subjects, levels, components and sessions can have different thresholds.
- Historical boundaries are useful reference points, not promises about future results.


A student uses an enormous telescope to inspect an exam result while a parent offers a tiny telescope


### Marks and IB grades are not the same thing


Imagine the student looking again at that 68%. The mark tells them how many available marks they earned after any relevant weighting. It does not independently explain the standard of performance represented by that number.


A boundary supplies that context. In a simplified hypothetical example, suppose the boundary for a 7 begins at 72 and the boundary for a 6 begins at 61. A final weighted score of 68 would produce a 6. If a different session had a 7 boundary of 67, the same score would produce a 7.


These numbers are illustrative only. They are not boundaries for any real subject or session.


This distinction matters because an assessment can be more demanding than intended even when it covers the correct syllabus. If every session used an immovable percentage threshold, students taking the harder assessment could be disadvantaged. Boundary-setting is intended to preserve the meaning of an IB grade by considering the demonstrated quality of work, rather than treating every paper as perfectly interchangeable.


For a broader introduction to the terminology, read[IB Grade Boundaries Explained](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-grade-boundaries-explained) .


### How IB grade boundaries are set in practice


The IB’s assessment guidance says that the principal method is reviewing the quality of candidate work against grade descriptors. Those descriptors express what performance at different grades looks like. In other words, the process starts with standards, not with deciding that a fixed proportion of students should receive each grade.


### Examiners review candidate work


Senior examining teams consider actual responses around possible thresholds. The important question is not simply, “How many students earned this score?” It is, “What level of achievement does work at this score demonstrate?”


This is why boundaries should not be understood as a ranking contest in which only a predetermined percentage may earn a 7. Overall result patterns can provide useful evidence, but the quality of work remains central.


### Grade descriptors anchor the judgement


Grade descriptors help examiners connect marks to levels of achievement. A boundary should distinguish between work that just meets the standard for a grade and work that falls just below it.


The process is necessarily more nuanced than feeding marks into a universal formula. Subjects assess different things. A mathematics response may accumulate marks through valid method and accuracy, while a literature essay is evaluated through analytical and written qualities expressed in assessment criteria. Both eventually produce IB grades, but the evidence behind those grades differs.


### Statistical evidence supports the decision


The IB also uses quantitative evidence to inform grading judgements. Statistical information can help examining teams identify unusual patterns, compare outcomes and test whether a proposed boundary is plausible.


But statistics support professional judgement rather than replacing it. A result distribution cannot, by itself, reveal whether an assessment was unusually demanding or whether the cohort produced stronger work. That requires evidence about the assessment and the work students actually submitted.


The IB has published research describing this as a combination of qualitative and quantitative evidence, with statistical information considered alongside examiner judgement and teacher insight. RevisionDojo’s guide to[how IB grade boundaries are calculated](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-grade-boundaries-how-theyre-actually-calculated) explores that relationship further.


### Why grade boundaries can change


The student with 68% now finds an old boundary table online. It is tempting to treat it as a conversion chart carved in stone. It is better understood as a dated record.


Every examination session contains different questions and a different global cohort. Even carefully designed assessments cannot be identical in difficulty. A question may involve a less familiar combination of ideas, place heavier demands on time or produce responses that are harder to distinguish at a particular level.


A changed boundary does not automatically mean standards became easier or harder. Sometimes moving a threshold is how a stable achievement standard is maintained across assessments of slightly different difficulty.


Several factors may be relevant:


Evidence considered What it helps examiners understand


Candidate work The quality demonstrated near a proposed threshold


Grade descriptors The achievement standard associated with each grade


Statistical patterns Whether outcomes or mark distributions appear unusual


Assessment evidence How the questions performed and where students struggled


Teacher feedback Whether there were concerns about an assessment’s demands


Students should therefore attach a full label to every example they use: subject, SL or HL, component, session and year. A May 2025 boundary, for example, describes May 2025. It does not establish the boundary for November 2026 or any later session.


### How components become a final subject grade


Most IB subjects combine more than one assessed component. These can include examinations, internal assessment and, depending on the subject, oral, practical or other externally assessed work. Each component has a prescribed weighting.

This explains why averaging classroom percentages can produce a misleading prediction. A component worth more of the final result has more influence. Raw marks may also need to be scaled before they contribute to the total.


Coursework marks can undergo moderation, which may adjust the marks awarded by a school so they align with the common IB standard. That is separate from boundary-setting, although both processes contribute to comparability.

### What students and parents should do with boundaries


Boundaries are useful when they provide perspective. They become harmful when they encourage false precision.


For students, the sensible approach is to practise with representative questions, apply the correct component weights and compare results with boundaries from the matching subject and session. Use several recent sessions where available. Build a safety margin rather than preparing to land on an exact threshold, because the next boundary is unknown until grading is completed.


For parents, a single percentage is rarely enough to evaluate progress. Ask which component was assessed, whether school grading used official criteria, how representative the task was and where marks were lost. “What should improve next?” is usually more productive than “What grade is 68%?”


The student at the beginning of this story wanted certainty from one number. What they needed was context. Marks show what happened on a task; boundaries interpret those marks against a standard; feedback shows what to do next.
